title: You Can't Do the Pushpa Step Anymore: Why Allu Arjun's 'Raaka' Team Is Copyrighting His Signature Moves
excerpt: In a first for Indian cinema, the makers of Allu Arjun's upcoming film with director Atlee are seeking legal protection for his character's dance moves, gestures, and dialogues — a strategy that could reshape how Bollywood and Tollywood monetise their biggest stars.
body:
Every Indian wedding DJ in Edison, New Jersey knows the move. The chest-tap, the hair-flick, the cocked eyebrow with the finger-gun — Allu Arjun's Pushpa swagger became one of the most replicated gestures in Indian pop culture, spawning millions of TikToks, wedding choreographies, and brand knockoffs from Bengaluru to Birmingham.

Now, the people making his next film want to make sure nobody profits from it but them.

## The Copyright Play

The producers of *Raaka*, Allu Arjun's upcoming film directed by Atlee (of *Jawan* fame), have announced that they are seeking legal protection for the character's signature dance steps, physical mannerisms, and catchphrases. If successful, it would be one of the first instances of a major Indian film production copyrighting specific performance elements — not just the film, the music, or the screenplay, but the way an actor moves his body on screen.

The strategy follows an expensive lesson from *Pushpa: The Rise*. When the film's signature moves went viral, they became the basis for advertising campaigns, stage shows, social media content, and merchandise — most of it unauthorised. Allu Arjun himself went to court earlier this year over the unauthorised use of his persona, and the *Raaka* team is determined not to repeat the cycle.

"We are treating the character's physical identity as intellectual property from day one," a production source told a Telugu entertainment outlet. "Every move, every dialogue delivery pattern — it will be documented and registered before the first trailer drops."

## Why This Matters Beyond Telugu Cinema

The copyright move is being watched closely not just in Hyderabad but across the Indian film industry. In Hollywood, character elements have been legally protected for decades — try putting a Batman logo on a T-shirt without Warner Bros. coming after you. But Indian cinema has traditionally treated viral moments as free marketing: the more people copied your hero's walk, the bigger your film got.

That calculation has changed. With streaming platforms, social media influencers, and brand partnerships worth crores riding on a character's cultural footprint, the economics of virality have shifted. A single unauthorised brand campaign using Pushpa's mannerisms could divert lakhs of rupees that would otherwise flow to the actor or the production house.

The *Raaka* team's approach borrows from the Pushpa playbook but formalises it. The film, which stars Deepika Padukone opposite Allu Arjun and is expected to be a pan-India blockbuster with a release across five languages, is being built as a character-brand from the ground up — merchandise plans, signature moves, catchphrases, and visual identity all locked in before the cameras roll.

## The Criticism: Are They Going Too Far?

Not everyone is thrilled. On Telugu film forums and social media, some fans have pushed back, arguing that copyrighting dance moves stifles the organic virality that made Pushpa a phenomenon in the first place.

"If someone in Rajahmundry does the Pushpa step at a wedding, are they going to get a legal notice?" one widely shared tweet asked. The concern is that overly aggressive IP protection could create a chilling effect on fan culture — the very engine that drives Telugu and Tamil cinema's enormous grassroots reach.

Industry observers note that the copyright filings are likely targeted at commercial exploitation rather than casual fan behaviour. No production house is going to sue a teenager on Instagram. But the branded content creators, the advertising agencies, the event managers charging for "Pushpa theme" shows — those are the targets.

## The NRI Connection

For diaspora audiences, this story hits close to home. Allu Arjun's international appeal — sealed during his triumphant Japan tour where he delivered Pushpa dialogues in Japanese to thunderous applause — means his character IP has value in markets from the US to the Gulf states. NRI wedding planners, event companies in London and Toronto, and South Asian content creators on YouTube have all built businesses around Telugu cinema's viral moments.

If the *Raaka* copyright strategy succeeds, it could set a precedent that reshapes how that value is captured and distributed — not just for Allu Arjun, but for every Indian star whose signature move becomes the next global trend.

The film is expected to begin shooting in late 2026 for a 2027 release. The legal filings, however, have already begun.
